content: A perceptual paradox occurs when a theoretical prediction fails to align with what is actually perceived. Theories of perception are designed to help researchers predict what will be perceived when sensory systems are stimulated. These theories typically include a mathematical model (a formula), guidelines for collecting physical measurements to input into the model, and rules for mapping the model's outputs to physical measurements. When valid input data is chosen, the model should reliably produce output data that matches the observed system. However, while these theories may be useful for limited predictions, they are generally unreliable for comprehensive modeling of perception across vision, hearing, touch, smell, and taste. A paradox highlights where such theoretical predictions fail. In some cases, even without a predictive theory, the characteristics of perception can appear nonsensical. A perceptual paradox, in its purest form, is a situation where a formula fails to predict what we perceive based on sensory inputs. A seemingly nonsensical characteristic refers to an observation that no existing theory has been able to explain. One branch of perception research involves using mathematical models to explain sensory inputs and predict perceptual outputs. For example, what we measure with our eyes should theoretically be predictable by applying formulas to measurements taken with instruments that mimic the eye. Past researchers have developed formulas that predict some, but not all, perceptual phenomena. Modern researchers continue to refine these formulas to address earlier shortcomings. Some formulas are carefully designed to replicate the actual structures and functions of sensory mechanisms, while others rely on assumptions about mathematical similarities. However, no perceptual formula has yet achieved the status of a natural law, like the laws of gravitation or electrical attraction. As a result, the development of perceptual formulas remains an active area of scientific inquiry. Historically, some Nobel laureates have contributed to the field by establishing principles of good scientific practice. Santiago Ramón y Cajal emphasized the importance of answering three key questions to validate a histological observation: the functional role of the arrangement in the organism, the mechanisms underlying this function, and the evolutionary and developmental processes that gave rise to these mechanisms. Allvar Gullstrand highlighted the challenges of treating the optics of the eye as if they were as predictable as camera optics. Charles Scott Sherrington viewed the brain as the crowning achievement of the reflex system, suggesting that all aspects of perception could potentially be explained by simple formulas applied to complex distributions. In sensory observations, the five primary senses—vision, hearing, touch, smell, and taste—are often studied alongside other sensory modalities, such as electrical perception. Similarly, perceptual observations are categorized by these senses. Statements of Perceptual Paradoxes: 1. Visual Contrast Invariance: Boundaries between brighter and darker areas appear to maintain constant relative contrast when the ratio of the logarithms of their intensities remains constant. However, logarithmic calculations are invalid for values that can reach zero, and no published neuroanatomical model predicts this phenomenon. 2. Color Constancy: Objects appear to retain their color regardless of the lighting conditions. For instance, an apple looks red whether viewed in direct sunlight, under a blue sky, during a sunset, or under artificial light. Edwin Land demonstrated this by illuminating a room with only two wavelengths of light (around 500 nm and 520 nm), yet observers perceived the room in full color. Despite this, no formula has been published that predicts the perceived color of objects in a single image under arbitrary lighting. 3. Transverse Chromatic Aberration: Light passing through a simple lens, such as the eye, undergoes refraction, splitting into colors. An off-center white light source projects a pattern with color separation along a radial line. Despite this, a white pixel on a screen appears white even when viewed at an angle. No neuroanatomical model explains this perception. 4. Longitudinal Chromatic Aberration: Similar to transverse chromatic aberration, the RGB components of a white pixel project to different focal lengths, creating a bullseye-like color distribution. Yet, no model predicts the perception of a centered white pixel. 5. Spherical Aberration: The cornea and lens of the eye are not perfectly spherical, leading to a non-circular distribution of photons on the retina. No neuroanatomical model predicts the perception of this non-circular distribution. 6. Hyperacuity: Humans can perceive distinctions finer than what would be expected based on the spacing of photoreceptors. For example, some individuals can achieve hyperacute vision with discrimination measured at less than one-tenth the radius of a single photoreceptor. This includes tasks like vernier discrimination of adjacent lines or distinguishing two stars in the night sky. No model predicts the ability to discriminate between two white pixels closer together than a single photoreceptor. 7. Pupil Size Inversion: When pupils narrow to around 1 mm for reading fine print, the central Airy disk increases in size, theoretically increasing blur. However, discrimination improves under these conditions, contrary to expectations. No model explains this phenomenon. 8. Pupil Shape Inversion: Human pupils are rarely perfectly circular, and other species exhibit a variety of pupil shapes, such as vertical slits in cats, horizontal rectangles in goats, or complex shapes in cuttlefish. No model predicts the perception of white pixels distributed according to these diverse pupil shapes. These paradoxes highlight the limitations of current theoretical models in fully explaining the complexities of human and animal perception.
